OWNER SPECIFICATION REVIEW EVENT, r11 R11-001 / R11-002 (the two ledger rows naming one
defect; R11-003 is their registered duplicate), 2026-09-16. Recorded under the r11 closure mandate's AFK review authority. THM-0118
is in NO declared root's transitive closure — verified, not assumed — so this is an ordinary
claim correction rather than a published-surface review event.

WHAT MOVED: `statement` and `scope`. `security_consequence` is unchanged.

THE DEFECT. The statement named the key as the verified triple `(signer, principal, nonce)`
and said a nonce "accounted to a different principal" is fresh. The code keys on
`(signer, audience, nonce)`:

    ReplayCache::check_and_insert(&self, signer, audience, nonce, expires_at_unix)
    InMemoryReplayCache            key = (signer, audience, nonce)
    AsyncReplayTier                composite_replay_key(&key.signer, &key.audience, &key.nonce)

`ReplayKey::principal` never reaches the cache. Its one consumer is
`Charge::reserve(&self.ledger, &key.principal, …)` — the retention budget — and it is
deliberately absent from `composite_replay_key`.

WHICH IS WRONG: THE CLAIM, in two places at once. The unit description of
`core.replay_seam` carried the same wrong triple, so the registry agreed with itself and with
nothing else. Both are corrected; `ReplayKey::principal`'s own doc at `replay.rs:118-124`
already argued the real design correctly and at length, which is what makes this a prose
defect rather than a code one.

THE EVIDENCE WAS ALREADY RIGHT, and that is the sharpest part. The registered controls are
`different_audience_same_nonce_is_fresh` and `different_signer_same_nonce_is_fresh`. There is
no principal control and there never was, because the cache has no principal discriminator to
measure — so the battery established the REAL triple while the prose asserted another. A
reader auditing replay scope would have checked the wrong field and found the tests silent
about it.

Neither direction of the old text was safe to leave. It asserted a freshness that does not
exist — two requests alike but for the principal are ONE entry, not two — and it omitted
`audience`, which is a discriminator the code really has. The scope now says what the
principal IS, so the next reader does not have to rediscover it: what a principal may occupy
is the async tier's question, and this claim is about which requests collide rather than
about who pays for the collision space.
